<reason>Both sides were disciplined and evenly grounded. CON's central dilemma — the mandated number is either misleading or invented — was the sharpest weapon of the debate, but PRO defused it cleanly in Rebuttal 2: the mandate covers three cash facts (paid/got/retained) that are exact to the cent, with platforms free to itemize costs beneath. CON's fallback ("a fact stripped of context is a rhetorical weapon") was plausible but assertion-heavy, and CON slightly mischaracterized PRO as having "conceded" that honest per-ride numbers cannot exist. On driver decision-making, CON's "own earnings history" rebuttal neutralized PRO's airport/short-hop example, yet PRO's broader labor-market framing — detecting algorithmic wage cuts, pricing one's own labor — was never fully answered, and PRO's Q2 trap (either the split kills trips because it's exploitative, or it doesn't kill them) forced CON into a third-horn behavioral-bias story that PRO reframed as "ignorance as a business model." Both handled pressure questions with proper A1/A2 format and direct answers. PRO's closing crystallized the stakes more memorably, while CON's closing leaned on recap of the dilemma plus the vivid torch metaphor. A close, well-executed debate with a clear but competitive edge to PRO on resolving the decisive clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 answer to the false-dilemma pressure question: "retained is cash movement, exact to the cent, not accounting" dissolved CON's misleading-vs-invented dilemma, and PRO's Q2 (why does seeing $25 kill a fair $14 trip unless the split is exploitative?) forced CON into conceding drivers would irrationally reject profitable work — which PRO then flipped into evidence that the system depends on blindness.</best_rebuttal>
